items.headline: Study finds exoplanet systems fall into two distinct families
items.title: Planetary systems reveal two distinct families tied to their host stars
items.scifi_hook: Astronomers discover planetary families that mirror the diversity of alien civilizations.
items.eli5: Researchers saw that groups of planets around stars cluster into two clear types.
items.why: It reshapes how we model planet formation and search for life.
items.text: Analyzing a sample of 300 of the best-characterized planetary systems among the more than 1,000 known in the Milky Way, an international research team led by the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics (INAF) has discovered that the multiplanet systems identified so far belong to two distinct "families."

items.headline: Voyager Technologies’ Griffin-1 lunar lander passes JPL environmental tests
items.title: NASA JPL Testing Readies Voyager Technologies Lander for Moon Mission
items.scifi_hook: A commercial moon lander proves it can survive the vacuum, heat and roar of a lunar launch.
items.eli5: The Griffin-1 lander was tested in a big simulator to make sure it can handle space and moon conditions.
items.why: Successful tests move the lander closer to supporting NASA’s first lunar outpost.
items.text: 4 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Engineers and technicians use a crane to position Voyager Technologies’ Griffin-1 lunar lander within the 25-Foot Space Simulator at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory on Aug. 31. The spacecraft recently completed a series of rigorous environmental tests at JPL ahead of launch to the Moon later this year. NASA/JPL-Caltech The testing team moves Voyager Technologies’ Griffin-1 through a hallway to the 25-Foot Space Simulator at JPL. The corridor features photos of the historic spacecraft that have been tested in the facility since the 1960s, from the Ranger program to NASA’s Europa Clipper. NASA/JPL-Caltech A commercial lander that will be at the forefront of NASA’s efforts to establish a Moon Base, humanity’s first lunar outpost, has passed a series of critical tests at the agency’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. The tests simulated the extreme temperatures and vacuum of space, as well as the intense shaking and ear-splitting roar of launch. Results show that Voyager Technologies’ Griffin Mission One (Griffin-1) spacecraft is ready to survive the rigors of space exploration. As part of NASA’s CLPS (Commercial Lunar Payload Services) initiative within the Moon Base Program, Griffin-1 is expected to launch later this year aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket. items.headline: SpaceX CRS-35 delivers ROSA solar arrays built by Redwire to ISS
items.title: SpaceX launches NASA science and cargo to the International Space Station
items.scifi_hook: Redwire’s fold‑out solar wings hitch a ride to the space station on a SpaceX cargo mission.
items.eli5: Redwire made small solar panels that were packed on a SpaceX Dragon and will be installed on the ISS.
items.why: Adds power to the station and showcases Redwire’s space‑hardware business.
items.rationale: Redwire could see revenue growth from ROSA sales
items.text: A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket’s booster and upper stage plume intermingle and are illuminated by the rising Sun during the launch of NASA’s SpaceX CRS-35 mission on Oct. 13, 2026. Image: Michael Cain/Spaceflight Now Under the soft glow of sunrise Tuesday morning, SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket roared away from pad 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 6:33 a.m. EDT (1033 UTC) to begin a cargo run to the International Space Station. The 35th Commercial Resupply Services (CRS-35) is carrying more than 6,300 pounds of science and supplies to the orbiting outpost when it docks to the space-facing port of the Harmony module on Thursday morning. Fewer than 7.5 minutes after leaving the launch pad, the first stage booster, tail number B1096, wrapped up its eighth trip to space and back with a landing at Landing Zone 40 adjacent to the pad. A thunderous sonic boom rang across the spaceport and beyond, signaling its return. Two minutes later, the Cargo Dragon spacecraft, tail number C211, separated from the Falcon 9 rocket’s upper stage to begin a two-day journey to the space station. Onboard cameras showed views of two Roll-Out Solar Array (ROSA) wings, nestled inside Dragon’s unpressurized trunk, that will be installed to augment the power of the ISS. Built by Redwire Space, these were the fourth and final pair of ROSAs bound for the space station. Each are capable of providing more than 20 kW of power for more than 10 years. items.headline: AI boom could push copper demand up 50% by 2040 and reshape pricing
items.title: Op-Ed: AI will not just add copper demand. It could change who sets the price
items.scifi_hook: Artificial‑intelligence data centers become a new, high‑paying copper customer, shifting market power.
items.eli5: AI needs lots of copper for servers and power lines, so demand may jump dramatically.
items.why: Higher demand in a tight market gives AI‑driven buyers leverage over copper prices.
items.rationale: Copper miners may benefit from rising AI‑related demand
items.text: Most discussions of artificial intelligence (AI) and copper focus on how many more tonnes of copper data centers will need. It is the right place to start, but it misses what may be the more consequential change. AI is bringing into the copper market a new class of buyer with an unusually high willingness to pay. As these buyers account for a growing share of incremental demand in a supply-constrained market, they could increasingly influence copper prices, reshaping who consumes the metal, how it is used and how the market evolves. A material-intensive start Despite its digital nature, AI rests on a substantial physical foundation that includes data centers, transformers, substations, cooling systems, new electricity generation and transmission lines. The International Energy Agency projects that global data center electricity consumption will rise from about 415 TWh in 2024 to around 945 TWh by 2030, more than doubling in six years. Industry estimates suggest that data centers may require roughly 30 tonnes of copper per megawatt of installed capacity, depending on design and the infrastructure included, before accounting for the wider electricity networks needed to power them. AI to boost copper demand 50% by 2040 — S&P AI is not arriving alone. It coincides with electrification, the energy transition and a geopolitical push to rebuild domestic manufacturing, diversify supply chains and expand military capacity. items.headline: Random mutations make RNA droplets behave like primitive cells
items.title: Random mutations turn RNA droplets into cell-like structures that move and store cargo
items.scifi_hook: Tiny RNA blobs mutate into moving, cargo‑carrying cell‑like structures.
items.eli5: A few random genetic changes let simple RNA droplets form cavities, move, and hold objects.
items.why: Shows how minimal chemistry could evolve toward life‑like functions.
items.text: A small number of random genetic mutations cause simple RNA droplets to transform into cell-like structures. In this process, they form cavities, can move and are able to take up cargo.

items.headline: Anthropic warns AI models could become self‑replicating worms
items.title: Anthropic warns of AI 'worms' spreading across smart gadgets
items.scifi_hook: Mini AI programs may soon crawl across gadgets like digital slime molds.
items.eli5: Small AI models could copy themselves from one internet device to another without human help.
items.why: Potential new vector for cyber‑threats across the connected world.
items.text: Small artificial intelligence models may be only months away from being able to behave like a computer worm, copying themselves from one internet-connected gadget to the next without human help, AI giant Anthropic said. An AI worm of this kind would likely be slow, taking days to copy itself, William Zhou and Daniel Freeman of Anthropic said, comparing it to a slime mold or a swarm of fruit flies.
